one_liner: Header-only C++11 Lua binding library without Boost; beat luabind on 8 of 13 rows of a 2018 shootout but trails sol2 and the raw C API.
what_it_does: LuaBridge exposes C++ free functions, classes, data members and properties to Lua, and gives C++ typed access to Lua values, from a single #include on top of PUC Lua 5.1-5.4 or LuaJIT. Registration is a fluent chain (getGlobalNamespace(L).beginNamespace(..).addFunction(..).beginClass<T>("T").addConstructor<void (*)(int)>().addFunction(..).addProperty(..).endClass()), conversions go through Stack<T> specializations (STL containers and std::optional via opt-in headers), and LuaRef wraps any Lua value for table indexing and calls. It is not a drop-in for luabind: the registration API differs, and overloads, enums, multiple inheritance and more than 8 parameters are unsupported per the manual.
how_it_is_fast: Each bound function compiles into a fixed template thunk (Call/CallMember, built from FuncTraits and TypeList) that reads arguments with Stack<T>::get and pushes the result; free-function pointers ride as lightuserdata upvalues and member pointers are placement-new'd into userdata, so a call does no overload matching (overloads are unsupported) and needs no Boost. Class instances get a metatable whose __index metamethod rawgets methods, then looks up the propget table and lua_calls a getter, walking the parent chain, and Userdata::get type-checks by walking class tables in the registry. LuaRef keeps every value in the registry (luaL_ref and luaL_unref per temporary), and C++-to-Lua calls go through pcall, which is why its table-access and Lua-function-call rows are slow next to the plain C API.
when_to_use: Replacing luabind to drop Boost: in the 2018 shootout LuaBridge was faster on global and table reads (table_get 102.5 vs 224.6 ns) and optional-value checks (optional_failure 22.5 vs 147.5 ns).
Existing codebases on the LuaBridge 2.x API that want a conservative, still-released line (2.10, October 2025) with vcpkg and Meson packaging.
Binding a moderate C++ API (single inheritance, getters/setters, static functions, up to 8 parameters) to PUC Lua 5.1-5.4 or LuaJIT with a C++11 compiler and no build step.
Mixed object lifetimes: values copied into Lua, raw pointers with C++ lifetime, or shared lifetime through RefCountedObjectPtr/RefCountedPtr.
when_not_to_use: Binding overhead is the bottleneck: in the same shootout LuaBridge is 15th of 16 on member_function_call (21,449 ns vs sol3 6,836 and plain C 5,469), last of 14 on lua_function_in_c (131.8 vs 32.9 ns) and 12th of 13 on multi_return_lua (8,161 vs 2,850 ns); sol2/sol3 or LuaBridge3 are faster on most rows.

APIs that need overloaded functions or constructors, enumerated constants, multiple inheritance, more than 8 parameters, or std::shared_ptr crossing the boundary (the manual says standard smart pointers 'will not work' and lead to undefined behaviour).
C++ calls into Lua functions that return several values: LuaRef::operator() runs pcall with one result and returns a single LuaRef.
Multi-threaded hosts using RefCountedPtr: its counts live in one function-static std::unordered_map with no lock, shared by all lua_States.

Hosts that cannot tolerate open crash and undefined-behaviour reports: #308 (crash passing a userdata metatable to luaL_tolstring), #289 (crash in Stack<int>::get), #296 (undefined-behaviour and stack-use-after-scope reports when running the tests) and #323 (clang 18/19 leak in readOnlyError) are open among 47 issues.

integration.dependencies: Lua 5.1-5.4 or LuaJIT headers and library (include lua.hpp yourself before LuaBridge.h); nothing else
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (C++17 optional via LUABRIDGE_CXX17 for std::optional and std::string_view); CMake 3.10 only for the unit tests
integration.platforms: any platform with a C++11 compiler and Lua; tests cover Lua 5.1.5, 5.2.4, 5.3.6 and 5.4.4 on Linux, macOS, MinGW/MSYS2 and MSVC
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. A lua_State is single-threaded and LuaBridge adds no locking; RefCountedPtr's global reference-count map is unsynchronized, so it is unsafe across threads even with separate states.

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the numbers: the shootout run (2018-09-28) shallow-cloned LuaBridge master between fc224ab (2018-09-16, 'Take care of LuaRef::Proxy', which removed the table proxy and shipped as release 2.1) and 74992b8 (2018-10-11, 'Restore LuaRef table proxy'). In that window operator[] returned a value copy, so t["k"] = v silently assigned to a temporary (issue #171: 'you can't actually change any table values from C++'); LuaBridge's table_set and table_chained_set rows are not unsupported but failed the harness check with 'unexpected result', and table_get, table_chained_get and the optional_* rows timed a proxy-less read path that 2.1.1 replaced.

The headline 7.1x win (table_global_string_set 15.7 vs 110.9 ns) compares LuaBridge's setGlobal helper, a bare push plus lua_setglobal that ties the plain C API (15.1 ns), with luabind's globals(L)["value"] = v proxy object; LuaBridge's own getGlobal path, which builds a registry-backed LuaRef, is 7x slower than its set (112.3 ns). The published JSON also does not match the committed harness: luabridge.cpp marks implicit_inheritance unsupported, yet the JSON holds a timed row (median 16,497 ns).

Every LuaRef and table item holds registry references (a current TableItem takes two, for table and key, and releases them in its destructor), so C++-side table access in hot loops costs several registry operations; drop to Stack<T> or the C API there.

Conversions report type errors through lua_error (a longjmp) unless the host calls enableExceptions or wraps calls in pcall; the manual says code must be wrapped in lua_pcall or use a throwing panic handler to be safe, and a lua_State* parameter must come last in a bound signature or behaviour is undefined.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: sol2/sol3 (the shootout author's own library) is faster on most rows, and LuaBridge3, a fork of this repository, beats vanilla LuaBridge on 12 of 22 shared cases in its own chart and adds features; pick vanilla LuaBridge only to stay on the 2.x API with minimal change or when moving off luabind with the smallest header set. nanobind binds Python, not Lua, so it is not an alternative.
verified_claims_summary: ThePhD's lua-bindings-shootout (Google Benchmark medians, Windows x64 release build with MSVC /std:c++latest, PUC Lua 5.3.4, 8 logical CPUs at 2592 MHz with no CPU model or compiler version, run 2018-09-28) timed LuaBridge master as it stood between release 2.1 and 2.1.1 against luabind: faster on 8 of 13 shared rows (table_get 102.5 vs 224.6 ns, optional_failure 22.5 vs 147.5 ns) and slower on 5 (member_function_call 21,449 vs 15,695 ns, userdata_variable_access 24,414 vs 15,346 ns). LuaBridge is slower than the plain Lua C API on every row it shares with it, and those rows measured a release whose table writes through operator[] were broken.
status_note: MIT, header-only and still released (2.10 by dmitry-t on 2025-10-13 after a 10-month gap, 47 open issues), so it is easy to vendor, but the only third-party speed evidence is a 2018 run of a short-lived master snapshot that a few weeks later needed a fix to make table writes work.
